title: VCIWU holds National seminar on women in AI era, honours research excellence
excerpt: HYDERABAD: Veeranari Chakali Ilamma Women’s University held a National Seminar called “Women in the AI Era – Empowering Future Leaders” on October 3, 2026. This event was part of the 131st Birth Anniversary celebrations of Veeranari Chakali Ilamma, with the theme “Remembering Her Life, Celebrating Her Spirit.” The event was organized by the BC Cell, […] HYDERABAD: Veeranari Chakali Ilamma Women's University held a National Seminar called "Women in the AI Era – Empowering Future Leaders" on October 3, 2026. This event was part of the 131st Birth Anniversary celebrations of Veeranari Chakali Ilamma, with the theme "Remembering Her Life, Celebrating Her Spirit." The event was organized by the BC Cell, SC/ST Cell, Minorities Cell, and Women's Studies Centre. Among the notable participants, Prof. Sangita Srivastava, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Allahabad, was the Chief Guest. Smt. Sri Devasena, IAS, Commissioner of Collegiate Education, Telangana, was the Guest of Honour. In their speeches, the speakers talked about the need for digital skills, inclusive education, responsible use of AI, and more women in technology, research, and leadership. Prof. Surya Dhananjay, Vice-Chancellor of VCIWU, said women should get involved with AI by using creativity, critical thinking, values, and innovation. Similarly, Prof. G. Mallesham, Registrar, explained how higher education helps students prepare for new technology and talked about the University's digital projects. Prof. Sangita Srivastava talked about women's rights, strength, and their role in national progress. In addition, Smt. Sri Devasena said that courage, determination, and natural intelligence should go along with artificial intelligence, taking inspiration from Veeranari Chakali Ilamma. Organisers and resource persons Dr. G. Vijayalakshmi, OSD to the Vice-Chancellor, served as Co-Patron, and Dr. Bangari Shailaja, Director, BC Cell, was the Convenor. Mrs. Chityala Swetha Ilamma, Member, Telangana State Women's Commission, and Prof. Pillalamarri Ramulu, University of Hyderabad, participated as resource persons. The event also included the release of the College Handbook and Centenary Alumni Magazine. The Vice-Chancellor Research Awards–2026 were also presented. Research awardees In the Faculty of Science, the awardees were Dr. Loka Pavani, Dr. Rupasree Mukhopadhyay, and Dr. S. Annapurna. Meanwhile, for the Faculty of Arts, the awards went to Dr. Syeda Naseem Sultana and Dr. Ramesh Singisala. In Social Sciences, Dr. Vinita Pandey received the award, and in Commerce and Business Management, Dr. Rajagopal was honored. Research Awards–2026 for Patents were given to Dr. V. Shashikala, Dr. G. Vijaya Lakshmi, Dr. Y. Sunila Kumari, Dr. Rupasree Mukhopadhyay, Dr. G. Sriramulu, Dr. T. Shekar Reddy, Dr. Spoorthi Veera, Dr. P. Nagaraju, and Dr. Ayub Shaik. In addition, awards for Projects went to Dr. K. Premalatha of the Department of Chemistry and Dr. Vinita Pandey of the Department of Sociology. The awards showed VCIWU's commitment to research, innovation, and academic excellence in many areas. The seminar ended with a call for women to learn new technologies, build their skills, and become leaders in creating a fair and creative future, inspired by Veeranari Chakali Ilamma's courage and legacy. ]]>

title: Building resilience not a one-time exercise, must keep at it: FM
excerpt: Uncertainty is now a standing condition of the global economy and policy must be designed around it, said Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.“We need to keep building resilience as we go along; it is not a one-time exercise,” she said at the fifth Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi on Saturday.The conclave, organised by the Institute of Economic Growth in partnership with the finance ministry, is being held from October 3-5 under the theme “Resilience in an Age of Flux”.The FM exhorted economists to look beyond headline growth when they judge how an economy handles shocks.The evidence of resilience is often counterfactual, it lies in the outcomes that did not materialise, she said. “…An inflation spiral that did not take hold, queues that did not form at fuel outlets, banking stress that did not surface and a fiscal correction that was never forced.”“These counterfactuals deserve as much attention from economists as the headline growth rate,” she said.The world has seen primarily two kinds of shocks over the past four years: crude price spikes and tighter US monetary conditions, she said.Also Read: India’s inflation inches closer to 5 percent. Is an October rate hike imminent?“The conflicts involving Russia, Ukraine and Iran, and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, added a new kind of shock, one that threatened the physical movement of oil and gas as well as their prices.”These shocks arrived at a time when the world had thin buffers.Global public debt rose to nearly 94 percent of GDP in 2025 and is projected to reach 100 percent by 2029, a level previously seen only after the Second World War.India has managed the weather these shocks well, she said.India’s economy grew 7.8 percent in the April-June (Q1) quarter of this fiscal when current account deficit (CAD) was 0.5 percent of GDP. Bad loans at banks are at a multi-decade low, and foreign-exchange reserves are about $766 billion.The FM listed the government’s focus on efficient last-mile delivery, infra spending, reforms, fiscal prudence, entrepreneurship, and the capacity to maintain economic continuity through disruption as some of the steps that have helped build resilience.On the future challenges, she said India approaches the coming years from a position of strength.Building resilient supply chains and global openness are two of the key priorities. “Global economic relationships must remain open, predictable, and rules-based,” the FM said.On the impact of AI on jobs, Sitharaman called for skilling the young people and urged industry to take a greater role in designing and delivering training.Also, private sector must now take over from the government as the main driver of investment, including spending on research and development (R&D), she said.The government has carried the capital spending cycle for most of the past decade.India spends 0.83 percent of GDP on R&D, compared with 2.7 percent across the OECD. Private companies account for only about 36 percent of that spending, she said.Her remarks add to the government’s long-standing push for companies to invest more.The government has budgeted Rs 12.2 lakh crore for capex in the Union Budget for FY27.Sitharaman highlighted the Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) scheme the government has designed to support the shift as India moves from “Made in India” to “Imagined and Made in India”.

title: Tighter financial conditions could spill over to banks, warns Sanjay Malhotra
excerpt: Any tightening of global financial conditions could spill over to banks and other markets, Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra said at the fifth Kautilya economic conclave in New Delhi, flagging rising leverage and stretched valuations as the main channels of risk.“High leverage in pursuit of high returns, and this is particularly true of the advanced economies [where] hedge funds, option sellers, exchange trade, traded funds, and other non-bank financial intermediaries have expanded leverage both in equity and bond markets,” he said, adding that rising leverage is a sign of maturing financial cycle. However, this is of “concern” especially since equity valuations are stretched and bank and NBFI interconnectedness has deepened both on the liability as well as on the asset side.Speaking on the interplay of monetary policy and financial stability, Malhotra further said that the RBI does not use monetary policy to address financial stability risks. “We follow the separation principle, monetary policy for price stability and targeted regulatory, supervisory, and macroprudential tools, where financial stability risks are identified.”He also noted that the financial system had absorbed the supply shock due to the West Asia conflict “quite well” and growth has been resilient.“However, the global economic environment continues to remain challenging. The conflict has exacerbated not only inflationary pressures but it has also elevated financial system vulnerabilities,” he added.Also Read: West Asia tensions begin filtering into Indian economy, says Finance MinistryThe RBI governor identified five global vulnerabilities. Global debt has risen, maturities have shortened and bond yields have hardened sharply, which could squeeze sovereign finances, strain corporate debt servicing and hit bank balance sheets through bond losses. Emerging markets with heavy non-resident holdings of sovereign debt could face outflows if carry trades unwind.Second, AI-linked asset valuations could be sharply repriced if the investment cycle slows. “As the investment cycle matures, any slowdown in AI investment or earnings could trigger a sharp repricing of financial assets, especially in the AI value chain. High risk appetite has spurred an increase in leverage, which, along with [a potential] decline in cash flow among major AI firms would further amplify market corrections and financial market volatility,” he added.Third, hedge funds, option sellers, ETFs and other non-bank intermediaries have built up leverage, deepening links with banks. Fourth, private credit has shown weak lending standards in some high-profile defaults. Fifth, AI is heightening cyber risk in a borderless financial system. Each may be manageable alone, he said, but a simultaneous hit could strain the global financial architecture.“Large differences in cyber capabilities and resilience and resolution capabilities across countries have implications for jurisdictions far beyond the source of the vulnerability,” he noted.For India, Malhotra said the exposure runs mainly through higher commodity prices and external-sector pressures. But he said the economy is navigating the phase from strength, with inflation averaging 2 percent last year and the fastest growth among major economies. Government bond yields have risen only partially, which he credited to fiscal consolidation and credible monetary policy. Equities have corrected from high valuations, but in an orderly fashion. An AI-led correction abroad could even draw capital inflows to India, he added.Malhotra called for better data, scenario analysis and system-wide resilience. “Today’s resilience may not necessarily imply tomorrow’s immunity,” he said.

title: How Bharat is expanding Ayurveda through public healthcare, insurance and telemedicine
excerpt: स्वस्थस्य स्वास्थ्यरक्षणम्, आतुरस्य विकारप्रशमनम् Protect the health of the healthy, heal the ailment of the sick. Nearly half of Bharat already uses Ayurveda or an allied Ayush system, often without calling it that. The National Sample Survey on Ayush (July 2022 to June 2023) found that around 46 per cent of rural and 53 per cent of urban Indians had used Ayush for prevention or treatment in the preceding year. Ayurveda alone accounted for 40.5 per cent in villages and 45.5 per cent in cities. Awareness touched 95 per cent. As the country marked the 11th Ayurveda Day on 23 September 2026 under the theme Ayurveda for a Healthier Tomorrow, the real story lies less in ceremonies and more in a simple question every family asks: where can I get genuine Ayurvedic care, will it be safe, and who will pay for it? What Ayurveda actually says The word Ayu means life, and Veda means knowledge. With roots traced to the Rigveda and a history of over 5,000 years, the system rests on two foundational texts, the Charaka Samhita and the Sushruta Samhita. Its purpose, spelt out in the Charaka verse above, is twofold: to keep the healthy well and cure the sick. Health, in Ayurvedic terms, is balance. The three bio-energies or doshas, the metabolic fire called agni, the bodily tissues or dhatus and the waste channels or malas must work in harmony alongside a calm mind, steady senses and a serene self. Treatment draws on plants, minerals and animal products, but diet, daily routine and seasonal living carry equal weight. That is why the NSS survey found Ayush being used chiefly for rejuvenation and prevention rather than only for cure, and why around 85 per cent of rural households know at least one medicinal plant or home remedy. Ayurveda Day was first observed in 2016 on Dhanvantari Jayanti, the Dhanteras festival honouring the divine physician. Because that date follows the lunar calendar, it shifted every year. In 2025, the Centre notified 23 September as a fixed date. It falls around the autumnal equinox, when day and night are nearly equal, a fitting symbol for a science built on balance, and it gives Ayurveda a steady place on the global calendar. Where can a citizen get Ayurvedic care today? For decades, the typical Ayurvedic dispensary was a small rented room with irregular supplies. That picture is changing through two missions working together: the National Ayush Mission (NAM) under the Ministry of Ayush and the National Health Mission (NHM) under the Health Ministry. Between 2014-15 and 2025-26, the Centre released over ₹6,406.99 crore to States and Union Territories through NAM alone. Ayushman Arogya Mandir (Ayush): Old dispensaries are being upgraded into wellness centres. As of 19 September 2026, 12,260 such centres were functional against a target of 12,500. NAM provides buildings, equipment and medicines, while NHM funds and trains the staff. Ayush counters now sit alongside allopathic care in 13,249 public facilities: 6,302 Primary Health Centres, 3,191 Community Health Centres, 475 District Hospitals and 3,281 other facilities. The government pays salaries for 25,322 Ayush doctors and 5,666 Ayush paramedics. A BAMS graduate can also serve as a Community Health Officer running a village-level centre. Premier central hospitals such as Safdarjung Hospital with VMMC and Lady Hardinge Medical College now house Departments of Integrative Medicine with working Panchakarma units, while Dr Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital hosts extended OPDs run by the Ayush Research Councils. The new AIIMS also offer Ayush services. NAM funds new integrated hospitals of 10, 30 or 50 beds, moves clinics out of rented premises and ensures a free supply of essential medicines. Public health drives and awareness campaigns built around preventive care and traditional wellness complete the package, taking the message beyond hospital walls. For those far from any hospital, the free eSanjeevani telemedicine platform, which has served more than 50 crore patients across all streams, includes Ayush OPDs. A farmer in a remote block can consult an Ayurveda specialist by video without spending a day and a bus fare travelling to the district town, and without losing a day’s wages. Will Insurance pay after treatment? This has long been the sticking point. The NSS data show that a rural patient spends around ₹394 a year out of pocket on Ayurvedic care, rising to ₹499 in cities. Three changes aim to ease that burden. First, in 2024, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) directed every insurer to offer products or add-ons covering all systems of medicine, Ayurveda included. Second, on 10 February 2026, the All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi, signed a common empanelment agreement with the General Insurance Council, linking it to all 32 general insurers for cashless treatment. No AYUSH institution had done this before. AIIA has also opened a helpline, 1800-11-0008, for insurance queries. Third, the World Health Organisation has added Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani terms to a module of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11). Doctors anywhere can now record an Ayurvedic diagnosis with a standard code, which makes claims easier to process and data easier to compare. Is it safe? The checks behind the bottles Herbal means harmless is a myth, and the law treats it as one. Ayurvedic medicines fall under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and the Drugs Rules, 1945. Manufacturers must follow Good Manufacturing Practices, meet pharmacopoeia standards and establish safety and efficacy. Drug inspectors sample products routinely, backed by a dedicated Ayush vertical in the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. The e-Aushadhi portal tracks manufacturing licence applications online. Food gets similar attention. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, working with the Ministry of Ayush, has notified standards for Ayurveda Aahara, with a list of authentic dietary products drawn from classical texts. For a consumer, the practical lesson is simple: buy from licensed manufacturers and consult a registered practitioner. Who is training tomorrow’s Vaidyas? An expanding network needs trained hands. title: Yami Gautam, Aditya Dhar leave Mumbai behind? Couple reportedly shifts to Himachal with son Vedavid
excerpt: Yami Gautam and filmmaker Aditya Dhar may have found a new home away from Mumbai. The couple, who have built their professional lives in the city, are reportedly choosing the quieter surroundings of Himachal Pradesh for their family. According to a report by Free Press Journal, Yami and Aditya have moved ‘permanently’ to Himachal Pradesh with their son Vedavid. They continue to have a rented apartment in Khar, Mumbai, and are expected to travel to Maharashtra whenever work demands it. Also Check: October 2026 Bollywood releases: Ajay Devgn’s Drishyam 3, Rajkummar Rao’s Prahaar, Yami Gautam’s Nayyi Navelli and more A Home Rooted In Himachal Before her marriage to Aditya, Yami had invested in a century-old heritage house and a 25-acre property in Gohar, Himachal Pradesh. Their home is reportedly surrounded by organic gardens growing apples, potatoes, plums and ginger. The property also holds special significance for the couple. Yami and Aditya got married there in June 2021. From Uri To Family Life The couple's relationship began during the making of Uri: The Surgical Strike. Their professional association eventually turned into romance, leading to their intimate wedding at Yami's family farmhouse in Mandi on June 4, 2021. In May 2024, they welcomed their first child, a son named Vedavid. However, Yami and Aditya are yet to officially confirm reports about their permanent move to Himachal Pradesh.
